title: Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I)
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the Scrum Guide 2020 and Scrum.org PSM I subject areas. Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A new Scrum Team is forming and wants to understand the core elements that make up Scrum. Which statement best describes what constitutes Scrum?
options: Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems
Scrum is a fixed set of processes that must be followed exactly to ensure project success
Scrum is a comprehensive methodology that prescribes detailed steps for every activity in product development
Scrum is a collection of best practices that can be applied independently without any specific rules
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide 2020 defines Scrum as a lightweight framework that helps people, teams, and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems.

items.stem: A development organization is considering adopting Scrum for the first time. How would they best characterize Scrum's approach to complexity?
options: Scrum works best when all requirements can be specified completely before any work begins
Scrum is designed to address complex adaptive problems where the path forward is not fully known in advance
Scrum is optimized for simple problems where requirements are stable and predictable throughout the work
Scrum is intended exclusively for technical maintenance tasks with clearly defined acceptance criteria
items.explanation: Scrum is founded on the understanding that complex work requires empiricism because the solution cannot be fully predicted in advance.

items.stem: As a Scrum Team begins their journey, they need to understand what makes Scrum effective. Which of the following best reflects Scrum's design philosophy?
options: Scrum requires teams to adopt every available agile practice to be considered truly Scrum
Scrum is a rigid prescriptive process that leaves no room for adaptation to specific contexts
Scrum is intentionally incomplete, defining only the parts required to implement Scrum theory effectively
Scrum provides exhaustive documentation templates for every role, event, and artifact in the framework
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide states that Scrum is purposefully incomplete, only defining the minimal parts needed to implement its theory while allowing teams to add practices as appropriate.

items.stem: A Scrum Master explains the foundation of Scrum to stakeholders. Which elements collectively form the basis of Scrum?
options: Scrum is built solely around project management principles with no underlying theory to guide its application
Scrum relies exclusively on waterfall planning techniques adapted for iterative delivery cycles
Scrum is based primarily on traditional command-and-control management theory for team coordination
Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking, implemented through its roles, events, artifacts, and rules
items.explanation: Scrum's theory is built on empiricism and lean thinking, and its implementation is guided by the specific roles, events, artifacts, and rules defined in the Scrum Guide.

items.stem: A new team member asks what Scrum Values guide the behavior of a Scrum Team. Which set of values should they be expected to uphold?
options: Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, and Courage
Efficiency, Predictability, Compliance, Hierarchy, and Discipline
Speed, Quality, Scope, Time, and Cost
Authority, Accountability, Control, Precision, and Consensus
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide 2020 identifies five values that guide Scrum Teams: Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, and Courage.

items.stem: When faced with difficult decisions during a Sprint, how do the Scrum Values influence the Scrum Team's actions?
options: The values require unanimous agreement before any decision can be made, regardless of time constraints
The values help create an environment of trust where difficult conversations can happen and decisions can be made transparently
The values encourage team members to avoid conflict by deferring all difficult decisions to a single authority figure
The values prioritize maintaining harmony over addressing important issues that arise during development work
items.explanation: Scrum Values create a safe environment for transparency and for having difficult conversations necessary for inspection and adaptation.

items.stem: A Scrum Team realizes their current way of working is causing friction. How should the Scrum Values guide their response?
options: They should escalate every disagreement immediately to management rather than resolving issues internally
They should prioritize meeting their commitments by suppressing concerns until after the Sprint ends
They should use courage to speak up, openness to share challenges, and respect to work through differences constructively
They should maintain silence to avoid disrupting team harmony and focus solely on completing assigned tasks
items.explanation: The Scrum Values are meant to be lived by the Scrum Team, enabling them to work effectively with each other and stakeholders, especially when facing challenges.

items.stem: An organization wants to ensure their implementation of Scrum truly embodies its values. What is the most accurate statement about Scrum Values?
options: Scrum Values are aspirational guidelines that are optional and do not affect how Scrum is performed
Scrum Values only apply to the Scrum Master and have limited relevance to the rest of the Scrum Team
Scrum Values are automatically achieved once the team follows the prescribed events and artifacts
Scrum Values are lived by the Scrum Team and must be demonstrated in their work, not just stated
items.explanation: When Scrum Values are embodied by the Scrum Team and the people they work with, the empirical Scrum pillars of transparency, inspection, and adaptation come to life.

items.stem: A team is transitioning from a traditional process to Scrum. What role do the Scrum rules play in this transition?
options: The Scrum rules bind together the roles, events, and artifacts, governing the relationships and interactions between them
The Scrum rules are suggestions that teams can pick and choose from based on personal preference
The Scrum rules exist solely to measure compliance and penalize teams for deviations from the prescribed format
The Scrum rules are only relevant during the initial adoption and become obsolete once the team gains experience
items.explanation: Scrum's rules establish the boundaries and interactions among the framework's elements to ensure empiricism is effectively implemented.

items.stem: A Scrum Master is coaching a team that wants to modify certain aspects of Scrum. What guidance should they provide?
options: There are no constraints on changing Scrum elements since every organization has unique needs
While specific tactics may vary, the Scrum framework's roles, events, artifacts, and rules should not be changed if they want to call it Scrum
Teams can remove any element of Scrum as long as they achieve the same business outcomes in a reasonable timeframe
Modifying Scrum is encouraged as long as the team documents their changes and follows their custom process consistently
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide defines Scrum's minimal elements; changing these core elements means the result is not Scrum.

items.stem: A stakeholder asks how Scrum differs from a traditional plan-driven approach. What is the key distinction?
options: Scrum eliminates uncertainty entirely by requiring all work to be defined and estimated before starting
Scrum follows a sequential phase-gate model but with shorter timeboxes than traditional waterfall projects
Scrum uses empiricism to navigate complexity, while plan-driven approaches assume predictability and try to control variables upfront
Scrum requires more upfront planning and detailed specifications than traditional project management approaches
items.explanation: Empiricism acknowledges that for complex work, more is unknown than known upfront, so learning through inspection and adaptation is essential.

items.stem: An executive wants to know what Scrum delivers. Which outcome best reflects Scrum's purpose?
options: Scrum's primary goal is to maximize utilization rates of team members across all available projects
Scrum focuses mainly on producing extensive documentation to satisfy compliance requirements
Scrum aims to complete every planned requirement exactly as originally specified, on time and on budget
Scrum helps teams generate value by delivering useful increments of working product that address complex problems
items.explanation: Scrum's purpose is to help people generate value through adaptive solutions, realized by delivering useful Increments of product.

items.stem: A Scrum Team is working with multiple stakeholders who have varying priorities. How does Scrum help manage these competing interests?
options: Scrum provides a clear ordering of work through the Product Owner and regular inspection opportunities to adapt based on feedback
Scrum requires stakeholders to form a committee and reach unanimous agreement before any work can begin
Scrum delegates all priority decisions to the Developers with no formal role for stakeholder alignment
Scrum avoids involving stakeholders during development and only engages them at the very end of the project
items.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value and ordering the Product Backlog, while events like Sprint Review provide opportunities for stakeholder feedback and adaptation.

items.stem: When explaining Scrum to a skeptical manager, which characteristic best distinguishes it from a heavyweight process?
options: Scrum mandates strict adherence to hundreds of prescribed practices with minimal flexibility for the team
Scrum is lightweight and relies on self-management rather than extensive upfront process definition and control
Scrum requires more detailed project plans, more documentation, and more formal sign-offs than traditional methods
Scrum introduces additional layers of management and approval gates to ensure tighter control over the team
items.explanation: Scrum is described as lightweight - it minimizes prescription and instead relies on self-managing teams and empirical process control.

items.stem: A new Product Owner is learning Scrum for the first time. What fundamental understanding should they have about the framework?
options: Scrum is a collection of agile techniques that can be implemented without any underlying framework structure
Scrum is primarily a toolset of software development practices rather than a framework for work
Scrum is not a process or technique; it is a framework within which people can employ various processes and techniques
Scrum is a specific project management methodology that must replace all existing organizational processes
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide clarifies that Scrum is not a process, technique, or definitive method - it is a framework within which various processes and techniques can be employed.

items.stem: A Scrum Team wants to improve their effectiveness over time. Where does the Scrum Guide suggest improvements should come from?
options: Improvements must be planned annually by upper management and cascaded down to all Scrum Teams
Improvements can only be made during a special 'improvement project' separate from actual product development
Improvements are prescribed by the Scrum Guide itself and must be implemented in a specific order
Improvements are identified through inspection at events like the Sprint Retrospective and implemented in subsequent Sprints
items.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective is specifically designed for the Scrum Team to inspect how they worked and identify actionable improvements for the next Sprint.

items.stem: A stakeholder is confused about accountability within Scrum. What is true about the three Scrum accountabilities?
options: Scrum defines three specific accountabilities - Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers - that together are responsible for Scrum's success
Scrum has a single Project Manager accountability who delegates work to the rest of the team
Scrum eliminates all formal accountabilities and relies entirely on consensus-based decision making
Scrum distributes accountability equally to every person in the organization involved with the product
items.explanation: In Scrum, there are three accountabilities: the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers. Together they form the Scrum Team and share responsibility for value delivery.

items.stem: An organization is trying to scale Scrum across multiple teams. What principle should guide their approach?
options: Scaling requires replacing Scrum roles with traditional management structures for better control
The fundamental elements of Scrum - its roles, events, artifacts, and rules - remain the same regardless of scale
Scaling requires eliminating certain Scrum events to reduce coordination overhead between teams
Scaling means combining multiple teams into one large Scrum Team with shared accountabilities
items.explanation: Scrum's core framework elements are consistent; scaling approaches may add coordination mechanisms, but do not change the fundamental Scrum elements.

items.stem: A new Scrum Team is establishing their working agreements. How should Scrum Values influence these agreements?
options: Working agreements should prioritize individual productivity metrics over team collaboration principles
Working agreements are unnecessary if the team simply follows the prescribed Scrum events
The working agreements should reflect and reinforce the Scrum Values of commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage
Working agreements should focus exclusively on enforcing penalties for missing deadlines and commitments
items.explanation: Living the Scrum Values strengthens working agreements and helps create a culture of trust, transparency, and continuous improvement.

items.stem: A manager asks why Scrum doesn't prescribe a specific project lifecycle or phases. What is the best explanation?
options: Scrum assumes projects are simple and don't require structured phases like traditional project management
Scrum eliminates the need for planning by delivering everything at once at the end of the work
Scrum is only suitable for maintenance work that doesn't require any distinct lifecycle phases
Scrum is designed for complex work where discovery happens continuously, so fixed phases would impede learning and adaptation
items.explanation: For complex problems, upfront phase definitions are often incorrect; Scrum uses Sprints as containers for iterative learning and value delivery.

items.stem: A Scrum Team is struggling with internal conflict. What role do the Scrum Values play in resolving it?
options: The values provide a common foundation for respectful dialogue, helping the team work through conflict constructively
The values require the team to vote and always accept the majority opinion without further discussion
The values suggest avoiding all conflict by having the Scrum Master make all decisions on behalf of the team
The values prioritize commitment over resolution, so conflicts should be set aside to meet Sprint Goals
items.explanation: Courage, openness, respect, focus, and commitment create the psychological safety needed to address conflicts directly and productively.

items.stem: When a team claims they are 'doing Scrum', what is the most important criterion according to the Scrum Guide?
options: They have completed Scrum training and obtained Scrum certifications for their team members
They are implementing the Scrum framework as defined - its roles, events, artifacts, and rules - while embodying its values
They hold all the Scrum events on the prescribed schedule, regardless of whether they produce value
They use Scrum terminology in their meetings, even if their actual practices differ substantially
items.explanation: To be considered Scrum, the implementation must include all framework elements and be guided by Scrum Values and theory.

items.stem: A Scrum Master is helping stakeholders understand their role in relation to the Scrum Framework. What is an accurate characterization?
options: Stakeholders are required to attend every Daily Scrum and provide direction to Developers throughout the Sprint
Stakeholders replace the Product Owner's accountability and make all decisions about the Product Backlog ordering
Stakeholders collaborate with the Scrum Team primarily during the Sprint Review and at other times as needed, while respecting the framework's boundaries
Stakeholders must be excluded from all Scrum events to prevent them from disrupting the team's focus and autonomy
items.explanation: Stakeholders are key collaborators and provide feedback, especially at Sprint Review, while the Product Owner remains accountable for backlog decisions.

items.stem: A new team asks why Scrum emphasizes cross-functionality. Which answer best aligns with the Scrum Framework?
options: Cross-functionality ensures each team member can do every job, eliminating the need for specialization entirely
Cross-functionality is primarily about having representatives from every department rather than creating a usable Increment
Cross-functionality exists to distribute administrative work evenly across all team members
Cross-functional Scrum Teams have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint without depending on others outside the team
items.explanation: Cross-functional teams possess the skills needed to accomplish the work of the Sprint, reducing external dependencies and enabling the delivery of a Done Increment.

items.stem: An organization accustomed to strict controls wonders how Scrum ensures quality without micromanagement. What is the answer?
options: Scrum relies on self-management, clear accountabilities, a shared Definition of Done, and empirical inspection to ensure quality
Scrum ensures quality by having a quality assurance manager approve all work before it is considered complete
Scrum eliminates quality concerns by moving so quickly that defects have no time to accumulate
Scrum relies solely on post-Sprint testing by a separate team to catch any defects in the delivered work
items.explanation: Quality is built in through self-management, the Definition of Done, and continuous inspection throughout the Sprint.

items.stem: A Scrum Team is debating whether to extend their Sprint length. What guidance from Scrum's design is most relevant?
options: There is no guidance on Sprint length as long as the team delivers something at the end
Sprints have consistent lengths less than one month to enable regular inspection and adaptation while limiting risk
Sprints should be extended whenever there is uncertainty to allow more time for analysis and planning
Sprint length should vary based on the complexity of each individual item being worked on
items.explanation: Sprints are fixed-length events of one month or less, creating predictability and enabling frequent feedback cycles.

items.stem: A Product Owner is concerned about transparency with stakeholders. How does the Scrum Framework support this need?
options: Scrum achieves transparency by creating extensive written status reports distributed on a weekly basis
Scrum relies on private one-on-one meetings between the Product Owner and each stakeholder to share progress
Scrum promotes transparency through visible artifacts like the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment, inspected at events
Scrum restricts transparency by only allowing the Scrum Team to see the details of work in progress
items.explanation: Transparency is one of the three pillars of empiricism, supported by clearly defined and visible artifacts that all stakeholders can inspect.

items.stem: A Scrum Master is coaching a team new to Scrum. What should they emphasize about the relationship between the framework's elements?
options: The events are the most important part, and the other elements exist merely to support scheduling and logistics
The artifacts are optional, and teams can succeed by focusing primarily on the daily coordination meetings
Each element of Scrum operates independently, so teams can adopt them selectively based on immediate needs
All elements of Scrum - accountabilities, events, artifacts, and rules - work together to implement empiricism and deliver value
items.explanation: Scrum is an integrated framework where roles, events, artifacts, and rules are interdependent and together enable empirical process control.

items.stem: An organization wants to measure Scrum's success. What is the most appropriate focus according to the Scrum Guide's intent?
options: The primary measure of success is the delivery of valuable, useful Increments that solve real user problems
Success should be measured by how closely the team adheres to the original project plan and schedule
Success is best measured by tracking the number of story points completed per Sprint over time
Success should be determined by calculating team member utilization percentages across all activities
items.explanation: Scrum aims to generate value; delivering working Increments that provide real value to users and stakeholders is its ultimate measure of success.

items.stem: A team is reflecting on whether they are truly living Scrum. Which question best aligns with the framework's essence?
options: Are we completing all planned work regardless of whether it still provides value to users?
Are we creating transparency, enabling inspection, and allowing adaptation to deliver valuable increments for complex work?
Are we following every step exactly as written in a prescriptive manual without making any adjustments?
Are we minimizing all forms of change by locking down requirements as early as possible?
items.explanation: At its core, Scrum is about enabling empiricism - transparency, inspection, and adaptation - to navigate complex work and generate value.

items.stem: A Scrum Master is explaining the foundation of Scrum to a new team. What is the core theory upon which Scrum is built?
options: Scrum is founded on reductionism, which breaks complex problems into isolated components solved independently
Scrum is founded on perfectionism, which requires all work to be defect-free before moving to the next phase
Scrum is founded on empiricism, which asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed
Scrum is founded on determinism, which assumes all outcomes can be predicted with sufficient upfront planning and analysis
items.explanation: Empiricism means knowledge comes from experience and decisions are made based on observed facts, which is essential for navigating complex work.

items.stem: For empiricism to work effectively in Scrum, certain conditions must be present. What are the three pillars of empirical process control?
options: Planning, Execution, and Verification
Analysis, Design, and Testing
Scope, Time, and Cost
Transparency, Inspection, and Adaptation
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide 2020 states that Scrum employs an iterative, incremental approach based on three pillars: transparency, inspection, and adaptation.

items.stem: A team notices their Increment has a quality issue that wasn't obvious before. Which pillar of empiricism is being exercised when they detect this?
options: Inspection, as they are examining the artifact to detect undesirable variances
Transparency, as they are making the work visible to external auditors only
Adaptation, as they are already changing the product based on assumptions
Planning, as they are creating new estimates for future work
items.explanation: Inspection involves examining Scrum artifacts and progress toward goals to detect undesirable variances.

items.stem: After discovering a significant issue during inspection, the Scrum Team adjusts their Sprint plan. Which pillar of empiricism does this adjustment represent?
options: Commitment, where they refuse to change direction despite new information
Adaptation, where the team adjusts their process or plan based on what was learned through inspection
Transparency, where they are disclosing information to stakeholders for the first time
Inspection, where they continue to examine the artifact without making changes
items.explanation: Adaptation means adjusting the process, plan, or materials if inspection shows that goals will not be met or if the resulting product is unacceptable.

items.stem: A Scrum Master is emphasizing the importance of making work visible. Which pillar of empiricism are they focusing on?
options: Adaptation, which works best when information is deliberately withheld from decision makers
Empiricism, which is separate from transparency and doesn't require visibility
Transparency, which ensures that aspects of the process and work are visible to those responsible for the outcome
Inspection, which requires keeping work hidden until it is perfectly complete
items.explanation: Transparency means significant aspects of the process must be visible to those responsible for the outcome so that inspection and adaptation are based on reality.

items.stem: Why is transparency critical for the other two pillars of empiricism in Scrum?
options: Transparency is nice to have but has no direct impact on the effectiveness of inspection or adaptation
Transparency slows down the process, making inspection and adaptation less frequent and less effective
Transparency only benefits stakeholders and has no effect on the Scrum Team's ability to inspect and adapt
Without transparency, inspection can be misleading and adaptation can be based on false assumptions
items.explanation: Inspection and adaptation rely on an accurate understanding of reality; if the work isn't transparent, decisions are based on incomplete or misleading information.

items.stem: A Scrum Team is working on a complex problem where requirements are evolving. How does lean thinking complement empiricism in Scrum?
options: Lean thinking focuses on eliminating waste and maximizing value, which helps the team focus on what matters most as they learn
Lean thinking emphasizes producing large batches of work upfront to achieve economies of scale
Lean thinking promotes adding extra features to increase perceived value regardless of actual need
Lean thinking requires detailed documentation for every step to avoid any form of waste
items.explanation: Scrum is founded on both empiricism and lean thinking; lean principles help reduce waste and optimize for value while learning through empirical cycles.

items.stem: When does adaptation become necessary in Scrum according to the empirical pillars?
options: Adaptation should be avoided as much as possible to maintain consistency and predictability
Adaptation is needed when inspection reveals that the process, plan, or product deviates from acceptable limits or won't achieve the goal
Adaptation should happen on a fixed schedule regardless of what inspection reveals
Adaptation is only required at the end of the project after all work is completed
items.explanation: Adaptation is triggered when inspection shows that aspects of the work or process are outside acceptable limits or will not achieve the desired outcome.

items.stem: A Scrum Team consistently discovers new information mid-Sprint that changes their approach. This is most aligned with which aspect of Scrum Theory?
options: This is a sign that Scrum is not appropriate and the work should be moved to a waterfall approach
This means the team should stop inspecting mid-Sprint and wait until the end to make any changes
Complex work cannot be fully predicted upfront, so empirical process control is necessary to learn and adapt
This indicates the team is failing at planning and should spend more time creating detailed upfront specifications
items.explanation: For complex adaptive problems, the path to the solution is discovered through doing the work - this is exactly why empiricism is fundamental to Scrum.

items.stem: How often should inspection occur in Scrum to support effective adaptation?
options: Inspection should only happen once per quarter to avoid disrupting the team's productivity
Inspection is limited to the Sprint Review and should not occur during the Sprint itself
Inspection happens only at the very end when all work is complete and ready for final delivery
Inspection occurs frequently through the five Scrum Events, each designed to inspect specific artifacts and progress
items.explanation: Scrum provides five events - Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective, and the Sprint itself - that create regular opportunities for inspection.

items.stem: A new Scrum Team is forming. According to the Scrum Guide 2020, which group makes up the Scrum Team?
options: The Scrum Team consists of one Product Owner, one Scrum Master, and Developers
The Scrum Team consists of a Project Manager, Business Analyst, Developers, and QA Engineers
The Scrum Team consists of a Product Manager, Technical Lead, and multiple functional specialists
The Scrum Team consists of stakeholders, managers, and the development team working together
items.explanation: The Scrum Team is a cohesive unit of one Product Owner, one Scrum Master, and Developers.

items.stem: What is a key characteristic of the Scrum Team's structure that enables them to deliver value?
options: The Scrum Team is governed by a steering committee that approves all work-in-progress decisions
The Scrum Team is self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how
The Scrum Team is managed by the Scrum Master who assigns all tasks and monitors daily progress
The Scrum Team is directed by the Product Owner who controls every detail of implementation
items.explanation: Self-managing teams choose how best to accomplish their work rather than being directed by others outside the team.

items.stem: In addition to being self-managing, what other structural characteristic does the Scrum Guide describe for Scrum Teams?
options: Scrum Teams are specialized, with each member focused solely on a single narrow technical discipline
Scrum Teams are matrixed, reporting to multiple managers to balance competing organizational priorities
Scrum Teams are cross-functional, having all the skills needed to create a value-adding Increment each Sprint
Scrum Teams are hierarchical, with clear reporting lines to ensure proper oversight and control
items.explanation: Cross-functional means the team has all competencies needed to accomplish the work without depending on others outside the Scrum Team.

items.stem: What is the optimal size for a Scrum Team according to the Scrum Guide?
options: A Scrum Team must have exactly 7 people to achieve optimal productivity as prescribed by Scrum
A Scrum Team should be as large as possible to maximize resource utilization across the organization
A Scrum Team must have at least 15 people to ensure sufficient diversity of skills and perspectives
A Scrum Team should be small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work, typically 10 or fewer people total
items.explanation: The Scrum Guide recommends having no more than 10 people total on the Scrum Team to maintain effectiveness and agility.

items.stem: If multiple Scrum Teams are working on the same product, what does the Scrum Guide say about their structure?
options: Multiple Scrum Teams working on the same product must share the same Product Owner to ensure a single Product Backlog and unified direction
Multiple Scrum Teams must have completely independent Product Owners to avoid conflicts between teams
Multiple Scrum Teams should each maintain their own separate product vision with no coordination between them
Multiple Scrum Teams require a separate Program Manager to override individual Product Owner decisions
items.explanation: When multiple teams work on the same product, they should share the same Product Owner and Product Backlog to maintain alignment and maximize value.

items.stem: What is the primary accountability of the Product Owner in Scrum?
options: Approving timesheets, conducting performance reviews, and managing team compensation
Maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team
Assigning tasks to Developers and ensuring they complete work on schedule
Managing the day-to-day activities of the Developers and resolving technical conflicts
items.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.

items.stem: A key responsibility of the Product Owner is managing the Product Backlog. What does this accountability include?
options: Estimating all work in hours and creating a detailed project schedule for the entire product
Approving code changes and enforcing specific technical architecture decisions
Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal, ordering items, and ensuring the backlog is transparent and understood
Writing detailed technical specifications and implementation instructions for every backlog item
items.explanation: Product Backlog management includes expressing Product Goal, ordering items, making them transparent and clear, and ensuring they are understood.

items.stem: The Product Owner may delegate parts of their work, but what remains true about their accountability?
options: Delegating work removes all accountability from the Product Owner for those activities
Once delegated, the Scrum Master becomes accountable for Product Backlog decisions
Accountability is shared equally among all stakeholders when delegation occurs
The Product Owner remains accountable for the value delivered and for proper Product Backlog management
items.explanation: Even if they delegate, the Product Owner remains accountable for Product Backlog management and maximizing product value.

items.stem: Who is ultimately responsible for deciding whether to release an Increment of the product?
options: The Product Owner has the sole authority to decide when to release an Increment based on its value
The Developers decide when to release since they built the Increment and know its quality
The Scrum Master decides releases based on the team's velocity and capacity
Stakeholders vote collectively to decide on each release of the product
items.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value, which includes deciding if and when to release Increments.

items.stem: What is the core accountability of the Scrum Master in Scrum?
options: Writing user stories, prioritizing features, and managing stakeholder expectations
Establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide and helping everyone understand and enact it
Assigning work to team members and tracking their daily progress against the plan
Creating project schedules, managing budgets, and reporting status to senior management
items.explanation: The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness by enabling Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide.

items.stem: How does a Scrum Master serve the Scrum Team in their day-to-day work?
options: By creating detailed work breakdown structures and enforcing strict adherence to timelines
By taking over development work whenever the team falls behind on their commitments
By coaching the team in self-management, removing impediments, and helping them focus on creating high-value Increments
By directing the team's daily activities and approving all decisions before implementation
items.explanation: The Scrum Master serves the team by coaching self-management, removing impediments to progress, and fostering environments that enable value delivery.

items.stem: How does the Scrum Master serve the Product Owner?
options: By overriding Product Owner decisions when they conflict with technical feasibility or team capacity
By writing all Product Backlog items and determining their exact order without Product Owner input
By managing the Product Owner's schedule and approving all external communications
By helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition, backlog management, and stakeholder collaboration
items.explanation: The Scrum Master helps the Product Owner with Product Goal clarity, effective backlog management, empirical planning, and stakeholder engagement.

items.stem: What is one way the Scrum Master serves the organization?
options: By leading and coaching the organization in its adoption of Scrum and removing barriers between stakeholders and teams
By enforcing organizational policies even when they directly contradict Scrum values and principles
By maintaining status reports for management and justifying the team's existence through metrics
By centralizing all decision-making authority for all Scrum Teams within the organization
items.explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organization by helping it adopt Scrum, understand empirical approaches, and remove organizational impediments.

items.stem: Who is accountable for creating a plan for the Sprint and for the quality of the work resulting from that plan?
options: External stakeholders are accountable for Sprint planning since they define all requirements
The Developers are accountable for creating the Sprint Backlog plan and for adhering to the Definition of Done
The Scrum Master is accountable for the technical implementation plan and overall code quality
The Product Owner is accountable for planning the Sprint work and ensuring technical correctness
items.explanation: Developers are accountable for planning how to accomplish the Sprint Goal and for instilling quality by adhering to the Definition of Done.

items.stem: What does it mean that Developers are self-managing within the Scrum Team?
options: Developers can unilaterally decide to extend the Sprint if they need more time
Developers are free to ignore the Definition of Done if they believe it is too restrictive
Developers decide how to turn Product Backlog items into a Done Increment during the Sprint
Developers have complete freedom to change the Sprint Goal at any time without consulting others
items.explanation: Self-managing Developers decide the best way to accomplish the work they have forecast for the Sprint.

items.stem: The Sprint is the heartbeat of Scrum. What is the maximum duration allowed for a Sprint according to the Scrum Guide?
options: Sprints must be exactly two weeks long
Sprints can last up to three months if approved
Sprints have no maximum duration
Sprints are timeboxed to one month or less
items.explanation: Aligned with Scrum Guide 2020 on Sprint timeboxing. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: During a Sprint, can the Sprint Goal be changed?
options: The Sprint Goal should remain intact unless it becomes obsolete
The Product Owner can change it anytime
Developers can change it anytime
It must change weekly
items.explanation: Sprint Goal stability is central to focus in Scrum. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: What happens if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete during a Sprint?
options: It continues until the planned end
The Product Owner may cancel the Sprint
The Scrum Master cancels it automatically
Developers must complete it anyway
items.explanation: Only the Product Owner may cancel a Sprint. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: What is the purpose of Sprint Planning?
options: To approve the budget
To conduct performance reviews
To plan the work for the Sprint and define the Sprint Goal
To review past work only
items.explanation: Sprint Planning establishes the plan and Sprint Goal. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Who crafts the Sprint Goal during Sprint Planning?
options: Only the Product Owner
Only the Scrum Master
Only the Developers
The entire Scrum Team collaboratively
items.explanation: Sprint Goal is created collaboratively by the Scrum Team. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: How does the Sprint Backlog relate to the Sprint Goal?
options: The Sprint Backlog is the plan to achieve the Sprint Goal
It is unrelated to the Sprint Goal
It must contain all future work
It replaces the Product Goal
items.explanation: Sprint Backlog is the plan for delivering the Sprint Goal. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Sprint Planning timebox for a one-month Sprint?
options: One hour
Eight hours
Four hours
Two hours
items.explanation: Max 8 hours for one-month Sprint. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of the Daily Scrum?
options: To plan the release
To assign blame
To inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan
To report hours to management
items.explanation: Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward Sprint Goal. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Who is required to attend the Daily Scrum?
options: Everyone in the organization
Only the Scrum Master
Only the Product Owner
Developers; others attend if working on items
items.explanation: Developers are required; SM/PO attend if working. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Daily Scrum timebox?
options: 15 minutes
30 minutes
One hour
No timebox
items.explanation: Always 15 minutes regardless of Sprint length. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Focus of the Sprint Review?
options: To close the project
To inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog
To sign contracts
To write test scripts
items.explanation: Sprint Review inspects Increment and adapts backlog. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Who can attend the Sprint Review?
options: Only executives
Only the Scrum Master
Scrum Team and key stakeholders invited by PO
Only Developers
items.explanation: PO invites key stakeholders. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Sprint Review timebox for a one-month Sprint?
options: Two hours
Eight hours
Six hours
Four hours
items.explanation: Max 4 hours for one-month Sprint. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?
options: To plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness
To calculate bonuses
To finalize budgets
To review resumes
items.explanation: Retrospective focuses on improving quality/effectiveness. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Sprint Retrospective timebox for a one-month Sprint?
options: Two hours
Three hours
One hour
Four hours
items.explanation: Max 3 hours for one-month Sprint. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: What is the Product Backlog?
options: A resource list
A risk register
An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product
A fixed schedule
items.explanation: Product Backlog is emergent and ordered. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Who is accountable for the Product Backlog?
options: The Scrum Master
The Developers
Stakeholders
The Product Owner
items.explanation: PO is accountable for Product Backlog management. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: What is the Product Goal?
options: A long-term objective for the Scrum Team
A daily task
A bug fix
A meeting agenda
items.explanation: Product Goal is the long-term objective. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Sprint Backlog composition?
options: Only defects
Sprint Goal, selected items, and a plan
All Product Backlog items
Only epics
items.explanation: Sprint Backlog includes plan to achieve Sprint Goal. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Who owns the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Scrum Master
Stakeholders
The Developers
The Product Owner
items.explanation: Developers own the Sprint Backlog. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: What is an Increment in Scrum?
options: A prototype sketch
Meeting minutes
An email
A usable stepping stone toward the Product Goal
items.explanation: Increment is usable and moves toward Product Goal. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: What does the Definition of Done describe?
options: Quality criteria for an Increment to be complete
Budget limit
Team size
Velocity target
items.explanation: Definition of Done defines quality criteria. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: When must an Increment be usable?
options: Never specified
By the end of each Sprint
Only at release
Quarterly
items.explanation: Increments must be usable each Sprint. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Who creates the Definition of Done?
options: The Scrum Master
QA alone
The Developers
The Product Owner
items.explanation: If no standard exists, Developers create DoD. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.

items.stem: Increments relation to Product Goal?
options: Unrelated
Final only matters
Each resets the goal
Each brings the product closer to the Product Goal
items.explanation: Increments progress toward Product Goal. This aligns with the Scrum Guide 2020.
